analysis.one_liner: Caps out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 a month for people with private health insurance.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced November 21, 2025, has only been referred to three House committees and has not moved since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require private health plans — employer plans, plans bought on the ACA marketplaces, and even bare-bones catastrophic plans — to cover at least one insulin product of every type and dosage form with no deductible and cost-sharing of no more than $35 for a 30-day supply (or 25% of the negotiated price, if lower). It counts rebates that middlemen like pharmacy benefit managers receive when calculating that cap. It does not change Medicare or Medicaid, which already have a $35 insulin cap under a 2022 law, and it does not apply to insulin products a plan does not designate as covered.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private insurance who use insulin — roughly several million Americans with type 1 and insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes — who would pay no more than $35 a month for their insulin, with nothing going toward their deductible first. Plans would also have to cover insulin before catastrophic-plan enrollees hit their deductible.

how_it_helps.text: Caps cost-sharing for covered insulin at the lesser of $35 per 30-day supply or 25% of the negotiated price net of all price concessions, including pharmacy benefit manager rebates, and bars applying the deductible to it [S2].

Requires every plan to cover at least one insulin product of each dosage form (vial, pump, inhaler) and each type (rapid-acting, long-acting, premixed, etc.), so no insulin user is left without a covered option [S2].
Applies to group health plans, individual market plans, and catastrophic plans, and requires the capped cost-sharing to count toward deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers who sponsor group plans would absorb the difference between the $35 cap and what patients currently pay, likely passed on as slightly higher premiums spread across all enrollees. Insulin users who buy non-selected or out-of-network products get no protection.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and premium payers generally

drawbacks.text: The cap only applies to insulin products each plan selects; a patient whose doctor prescribes a different brand or formulation can still face full cost-sharing, and out-of-network pharmacies get no protection [S2].

It caps what patients pay but does not cap what plans pay manufacturers and middlemen, so the underlying high list prices of insulin are untouched and the cost lands in premiums for everyone, including people who do not use insulin.
Plans may argue that mandatory rich benefits raise premiums and could push some employers or insurers to trim other benefits or drop coverage; the bill itself offers no funding to offset those costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it covers, this is a direct, immediate benefit: no insulin user in a private plan would pay more than $35 a month for their insulin. The costs are real but diffuse — modestly higher premiums spread across insured people and employer plans — and the design has gaps, notably the out-of-network carve-out and the fact that it rides on top of, rather than reforms, high insulin list prices. On balance the benefit to insulin users outweighs the broad premium cost, though a more complete fix would address prices themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House and split among three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce — and none has taken it up yet.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the Affordable Insulin Now Act on November 21, 2025, with four original cosponsors [S1] [S2].

The Speaker referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committees on Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce, for provisions falling within their jurisdictions [S4].
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote has been scheduled as of the latest action record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved the bill, which leaves the current system in place: private-plan insulin users keep facing full deductibles and cost-sharing, and health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers keep the present cost-sharing arrangements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Current cost-sharing practices continue for now

for.name: Rep. Angie Craig
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 21, 2025, capping insulin cost-sharing in private plans [S1] [S2].

for.name: 11 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including original cosponsors Reps. McBath, Horsford, Landsman, and Schrier [S3] [S2].

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on; no votes have occurred yet, so the partisan shape is so far one-sided.

industries.note: Plans must cover selected insulin with no deductible and at most $35 in cost-sharing, absorbing the difference between that cap and current patient payments. Patients who use insulin save; the cost is spread into premiums for everyone.
The bill counts PBM price concessions when calculating the 25% alternative cap, which limits how much rebate money can inflate what patients pay. It does not otherwise restructure PBM rebates.
Self-insured employer plans are covered through the ERISA and tax code provisions, so employers bear part of the added cost of the cap, which may show up in benefits negotiations.
Guaranteed coverage of one product per type and dosage form locks in a covered market channel, but the bill does not cap what manufacturers are paid, leaving their high list prices intact.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in three committees with no scheduled action; with 11 cosponsors, no Republican support, and only weeks elapsed since introduction, its most likely path is to remain in committee. An earlier House-passed private-insurance insulin cap (2022) died in the Senate without a vote, so even House passage would not guarantee an outcome. Its best realistic route is attachment to a larger health or funding package.
